title: Why Portimão tastes the way it does

lede.text: Portimão lies in a south-facing amphitheatre, with more than 3,000 hours of sun a year. Its reds are velvety and full-bodied, with the alcohol noticeable.

chapters.title: The Barrocal by the sea
paras: The appellation covers the municipality of Portimão in the Algarve. That means the parish of Alvar and part of the parishes of Mexilhoeira Grande and Portimão.
The vines grow in the Barrocal. The Atlantic Ocean and the Alvor estuary (the ria de Alvor) both reach them with a maritime influence.

fly.label: Ria de Alvor
fly.caption: The Alvor estuary, one of the two sea influences on the vineyards, along with the Atlantic.

chapters.title: Hot, dry and very sunny
paras: Its far southern position makes the climate markedly Mediterranean. So do a mountain barrier against cold northern winds and the south-facing amphitheatre.
It is hot, dry and not very windy, with very small temperature swings. Sunshine averages above 3,000 hours a year.
The harvest generally starts 8 to 10 days later than in Lagoa.

chapters.title: Sandstone and sand
paras: The soils are a big part of what sets the wines apart. They include thin soils on sandstone and Silves sandstone (grés de Silves), and sandy regosols.
There are also red or yellow Mediterranean soils on sandstone, and podzolised soils of coarse sands and sandstones.

chapters.title: Reds and whites only
paras: Portimão makes reds and whites only. Reds need at least 12% alcohol and whites 11.5%. The grape must has to reach the same strength naturally.
The grape list holds six whites, among them Arinto and Siria. It holds nine reds, among them Touriga Nacional and Negra Mole.
Vines must be at least four years past grafting. They are trained on a trellis about 0.50 to 1 m high, pruned as cordon (guyot) or as a goblet (taça). Yield is capped at 60 hl per hectare.
